lead: A blood cell does not conduct electricity well. Pull it through a small hole filled with salt solution and it pushes electrolyte out of the way. The resistance across the hole rises for a moment, so a constant current makes a small voltage pulse. Count the pulses and you have the number of cells. Measure their height and you have cell size. This is the Coulter principle. It turned the slow manual blood count into a routine automated test printed on every complete blood count report.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for a calibrated readout, and Unit 1 for amplifiers and transducers.

sections.h3: Blood cells and the manual count

blocks.text: Blood carries three formed elements. Red cells, or erythrocytes, carry oxygen. White cells, or leucocytes, defend the body. Platelets, or thrombocytes, help clotting. Adult reference ranges are wide. Red cells are about 4.5–5.5 × 10<sup>12</sup> per litre. White cells are 4–11 × 10<sup>9</sup> per litre. Platelets are 150–400 × 10<sup>9</sup> per litre. The five white cell classes are neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils.

Manual counting uses a haemocytometer: a glass slide with a ruled Neubauer grid and a chamber 0.1 mm deep. One large square is 1 mm × 1 mm × 0.1 mm, so its volume is 0.1 µL. Blood is diluted in an isotonic diluent so cells stay round and separate. The diluted sample fills the chamber by capillary action. A technician counts cells under a microscope in a known number of squares.

items: Dilute blood by a known factor D. For red cells D is often 1:200; for white cells 1:20.
Fill the Neubauer chamber and let cells settle.
Count N cells in a known volume V of diluted sample, in µL.
Use the formula below and report per litre.

blocks.where: N is the number of cells counted; D is the dilution factor; V is the counted volume in µL of diluted sample; 10<sup>6</sup> converts cells per µL to cells per litre.

blocks.text: A Coulter counter pulls diluted blood through a single aperture, about 100 µm across, in a glass tube. Two electrodes sit on either side of the aperture. A constant current flows through the electrolyte between them. A cell is a poor conductor compared with the electrolyte. As it enters the aperture it displaces conducting liquid, so resistance rises. The current source holds current constant, so the resistance change appears as a voltage pulse of a few millivolts.

The pulse is amplified and fed to threshold discriminators. A small pulse is a platelet. A medium pulse is a red cell. A larger pulse is a white cell. The thresholds are set from known size ranges and calibration particles. A scaler counts the pulses above each threshold. The same pulses feed a size histogram. The pulse height follows cell volume, so the histogram shows the population distribution.

blocks.where: ΔV is the pulse height in volts; I is the constant current in amperes; ΔR is the rise in resistance in ohms when a cell displaces electrolyte.

blocks.text: Two cells passing together make one pulse, not two. This coincidence loss makes a concentrated sample read low. Dilution to about 1:500 for red cells keeps the chance small. The aperture must also be clean; a clog blocks current and gives false counts.

sections.h3: Automatic counters and the white cell differential

blocks.text: A modern analyser combines impedance with flow cytometry. The diluted sample is forced through a narrow stream so cells pass one at a time through a laser beam. Forward scatter at a small angle gives cell size. Side scatter at 90° gives internal granularity. Fluorescence from a stained cell gives a chemical label. A detector array records all three for each cell.

A three-part differential groups white cells into lymphocytes, monocytes and granulocytes. A five-part differential reports neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils. Impedance alone separates by size only, so eosinophils overlap neutrophils. Optical scatter and cytochemical or fluorescent staining resolve them. The analyser plots a scattergram and flags abnormal populations for a manual film review.

Semi-automatic counters need the operator to dilute the sample and press a button. Fully automatic counters aspirate blood, dilute, lyse red cells for the white count, count platelets, and print a complete blood count. They also measure haemoglobin by photometry, as in 3.1. Results are reported per litre, with reference ranges by age and sex.

figure.caption: Diluted blood is pulled through a 100 µm aperture. Each cell gives a resistance pulse; the pulse height sorts red cells, white cells and platelets into separate counts.

spec.title: Coulter counter
spec.aria: Diluted blood is drawn through a small aperture; each cell crossing it produces a resistance pulse that is amplified, sorted by height into red cell, white cell or platelet thresholds, and then counted and plotted as a size histogram.

examples.question: A blood sample is diluted 1:500. While 0.2 mL of the diluted suspension passes the aperture, 2.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> pulses are counted. Find the red cell count per litre and per µL.
steps: Volume of diluted suspension counted V = 0.2 mL.
Cells per mL of diluted sample = N / V = 2.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> / 0.2 mL = 1.0 × 10<sup>7</sup> per mL.
Cells per mL of blood = 1.0 × 10<sup>7</sup> × 500 = 5.0 × 10<sup>9</sup> per mL.
Per µL is the same as per 10<sup>-6</sup> L: 5.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> per µL, that is 5.0 million per µL.
examples.answer: The red cell count is 5.0 × 10<sup>12</sup> per litre, or 5.0 million per µL.
examples.check:
counted = 2.0e6
volume_ml = 0.2
dilution = 500
per_ml_diluted = counted / volume_ml
per_ml_blood = per_ml_diluted * dilution
per_litre = per_ml_blood * 1000
print(f"{per_ml_diluted:.1e}")
print(f"{per_ml_blood:.1e}")
print(f"{per_litre:.1e}")

traps: Forgetting the dilution factor D. Multiply by it once; the diluted count is not the blood count.
Using the blood volume instead of the diluted volume in the formula. V is the volume actually counted in the chamber or aperture.
Reporting per millilitre when the report asks per litre. Multiply per mL by 1000.
Believing a high count from a clogged aperture. Coincidence biases counts low; a clog can bias them high.
Setting thresholds by eye. Platelets and small red cells overlap; set thresholds with calibration particles.

quiz.q: State typical adult reference ranges for red cells, white cells and platelets.
quiz.a: Red cells 4.5–5.5 × 10<sup>12</sup> per litre; white cells 4–11 × 10<sup>9</sup> per litre; platelets 150–400 × 10<sup>9</sup> per litre.

quiz.q: Name the five white cell classes.
quiz.a: Neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils.

quiz.q: Why does a blood cell produce a voltage pulse in a Coulter counter?
quiz.a: The cell is a poor conductor. It displaces electrolyte in the aperture, so resistance rises. With constant current, the resistance rise appears as a voltage pulse.

quiz.q: A 1:200 dilution is counted in a Neubauer chamber. 2000 cells are seen in a volume of 0.1 µL. Find the count per litre.
quiz.a: Cells per µL diluted = 2000 / 0.1 = 20,000. Cells per µL blood = 20,000 × 200 = 4.0 × 10<sup>6</sup>. Per litre = 4.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> × 10<sup>6</sup> = 4.0 × 10<sup>12</sup> per litre.

quiz.q: What do forward scatter and side scatter measure in a flow cytometer?
quiz.a: Forward scatter at a small angle measures cell size. Side scatter at 90° measures internal granularity.

quiz.q: A sample is accidentally diluted 1:50 instead of 1:500. Explain the effect on the reported count.
quiz.a: The sample is ten times more concentrated, so many cells pass together. Coincidence makes two cells count as one pulse, so the reported count is lower than the true value. The result may also exceed the linear range of the counter.

quiz.q: Why can a three-part white cell differential miss eosinophilia?
quiz.a: A three-part differential groups by size and granularity into lymphocytes, monocytes and granulocytes. Eosinophils overlap neutrophils in impedance size, so they are not separated. A five-part differential needs optical scatter, fluorescence or cytochemical staining.

beyond: Not for the exam. Routine counters now add reticulocyte and immature platelet counts by fluorescence. Point-of-care devices use microfluidic impedance and image-based cell recognition. Laboratories use autoverification rules and digital morphology to review flagged samples. Calibration is traceable to reference methods and control materials. Search for “Coulter principle microfluidics” and “digital morphology haematology”.
